Clothing Manufacturer Directories vs Going Direct: What Actually Works in 2026

✎ FABRIOZA Team 📅 July 26, 2026 🔄 Updated: July 26, 2026 ☕ 8 min read
Home › Blog › Directories vs Direct
TL;DR: Directories (Sewport, Maker's Row, Foursource) are excellent for discovering factories — but they add a matching layer, not a guarantee: vetting, sampling and QC stay your job, and platform-listed factories often quote higher to absorb fees. Going direct cuts cost and communication hops once you know how to vet. Best workflow: shortlist on platforms, then deal factory-direct with a paid sample and a small trial order.

Every founder starts the same way: googling "how to find a clothing manufacturer" and landing on a directory. Platforms are genuinely useful — we say that as a factory you can find on them — but they solve discovery, not trust. Here is how the options actually compare in 2026.

The Main Platforms

PlatformCoverageModelStrengthWatch out for
SewportGlobalPost project, factories bid (RFQ)Fast international shortlistingQuality varies by factory; vetting is on you
Maker's RowUSABrowsable directoryDomestic options, MOQs listed upfrontUS pricing; limited overseas reach

What Directories Do Well

Breadth and speed. In an afternoon on Sewport or Foursource you can collect five quotes across three countries — something cold-emailing would take weeks to match. Directories also surface specializations (denim vs knits vs outerwear) you might not know to search for. For US-only production, Maker's Row remains the cleanest starting point.

What They Don't Do

  • They don't manufacture. The factory does — and the platform's badge doesn't sew your seams. Sampling, QC terms and communication quality still decide your outcome.
  • They don't remove cost. Platform fees and success commissions are priced into quotes; the same factory contacted directly can often quote 5–15%% lower.
  • They don't finish vetting. Certifications, audit reports, sample rounds and payment terms remain your homework — our vetting checklist applies on-platform and off.

The Hybrid Workflow That Works

  1. Discover wide: post your project on a platform or two; collect 5–8 responses.
  2. Shortlist hard: keep factories with verifiable certifications (ISO 9001, amfori BSCI/SMETA), real product photos in your category, and MOQs that fit you.
  3. Go direct: contact the shortlist through their own websites; direct quotes remove the platform layer, and response speed tells you a lot.
  4. Pay for samples: a factory confident in its work charges for samples and credits it back on production.
  5. Trial before bulk: run a small production trial (we do 20 pieces) before any large commitment — it tests real production, not a hand-made showpiece.

When to Skip Platforms Entirely

If your product lives in a known cluster, go straight to it: sports uniforms and sublimation → Sialkot (our catalog); volume basics → Bangladesh; technical outerwear → Vietnam; printed wovens → India. Our country comparison series maps which cluster fits which product.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Sewport worth it for finding a clothing manufacturer?

Yes for discovery - posting one brief brings multiple international quotes quickly. Treat it as a shortlisting tool: the platform does not vet quality for you, so certifications, samples and QC terms remain your responsibility.

Is it cheaper to contact a clothing factory directly?

Usually yes. Platform fees and commissions are built into on-platform quotes, so the same factory contacted through its own website often quotes 5-15% lower and responds faster.

What is the difference between Maker's Row and Sewport?

Maker's Row is a browsable directory of US manufacturers with MOQs listed upfront - best for domestic production. Sewport is a global RFQ platform where factories bid on your project - best for comparing international options.

How do I avoid trading companies pretending to be factories?

Ask for a video call from the production floor, the factory's registered name and address, certification documents in that same name, and photos of your product category in production. Trading companies stall on floor access and paperwork.

What should I do after shortlisting manufacturers?

Order paid samples from your top two, compare construction and communication, then place a small trial production order (20-50 pieces) with the winner before committing to bulk. Never jump from sample straight to a large order.
